Questions

## Digital Product Passports in short

**Q: What is a Digital Product Passport?**

A Digital Product Passport is a structured data record about a product, reached through a data carrier such as a QR code. EU product rules make it mandatory product group by product group. It carries the information that authorities, repairers, recyclers and buyers need, such as composition, origin and how to repair or recycle the product.

**Q: Which products need a passport, and from when?**

Batteries come first: electric-vehicle batteries, light-transport batteries and industrial batteries above 2 kWh need a passport from 18 February 2027 under the Battery Regulation. Other groups follow once the Commission adopts their delegated acts under the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation. Its first working plan names textiles, furniture, mattresses, tyres, iron and steel, and aluminium. Until a product group has its delegated act, there is no passport date for it.

**Q: Where does a company start?**

With a readiness assessment. It shows which passport rules apply to your products and when, which of the required data you already hold, and which systems have to host, protect and register the passport. The compliance roadmap then puts that work in order against your deadline.

## Compliance Readiness Assessment

A readiness assessment answers three questions: which passport rules apply to your products and from when, which of the required data you already hold, and which of your systems would have to host, protect and register the passport.

### What you get

- The regulations and delegated acts that apply to each of your product groups, with their dates

- A gap table of the required data points against the data you hold today, and who holds the rest

- A check of your systems: hosting, access to the protected part, and registration

- The first three steps, in order

### Questions it answers

- Which passport rules apply to our products, and from when?

- Which of the required data do we already hold, and who holds the rest?

- Which of our systems would have to change?

### Often includes

- Mapping of the EU rules for each product group

- Data-gap scan against the required data points

- Short interviews with your own teams and key suppliers

**A good fit when** you know a passport is coming but not yet what it asks of you.

## Roadmap and Strategy

The roadmap puts the passport work in order against your deadline, with an owner for each step.

### What you get

- The steps from verification with a qualified seal to the first registration, in the order they depend on each other

- Data collection with your suppliers: what to ask whom, and by when

- The decisions you have to take first, such as build or buy

- A timeline your management can sign off

### Questions it answers

- What do we do first, and what can wait?

- Who owns each step, inside and outside the company?

- What do we need from our suppliers, and when?

### Often includes

- A register of requirements with the source for each

- Templates for supplier data agreements

- A workshop to agree the plan with management

**A good fit when** your deadline is fixed, as it is for batteries on 18 February 2027, or the readiness assessment is done.

## Supplier and Software Selection

A passport platform, a traceability tool or a data service binds you for years. We run the selection with you, so the choice rests on your requirements and not on the best demo.

### What you get

- A question set built from your passport requirements and your current systems

- A scoring matrix agreed before the first vendor answers

- The answers checked, with a right of reply for vendors on the points that decide

- A recommendation with the reasons and the risks written out

### Questions it answers

- Which platform fits our systems and our budget?

- How do we compare offers that describe the same thing differently?

- What do we lock ourselves into?

### Often includes

- A scan of the providers that fit your case

- The question set and scoring matrix

- A scoring session with your team

**A good fit when** you are about to buy a passport platform, a data tool or a service, and the offers are hard to compare.

## Passport Design and Implementation

We design the passport with your IT team or your passport provider and stay through the build, until a passport passes the Registry's checks.

### What you get

- A data model mapped to the Commission's semantic model where one is published

- Hosting and access design: the public part, the protected part and who may see what

- Validation against the published JSON Schemas and SHACL shapes

- Registration through the web interface or the API, and help choosing a provider if you buy

### Questions it answers

- What goes in our passport, and who keeps each data point up to date?

- Where is it hosted, and who may see the protected part?

- Which data carrier suits the product: QR code, NFC or RFID?

### Often includes

- Data model and IT architecture

- Data carrier choice and tests on the product

- A prototype passport, and a pilot on a real product with training for your team

**A good fit when** you are building a passport system or choosing who builds it.

## Business Value Beyond Compliance

Passport data makes repair, resale and take-back easier to run. We work out which of those models pay off for your products.

### What you get

- The circular models that fit your product and your market

- The passport data each model needs, and what you already collect for compliance

- A business case per model, with the assumptions written out

### Questions it answers

- Which repair, resale or take-back model fits our product?

- Which of that data do we already collect for compliance?

- What is it worth?

### Often includes

- Choice of circular model

- Advice on the footprint method (LCA, PEF) where a model needs one

- A business case with the assumptions written out

**A good fit when** you want the passport to earn something back, not only to tick a box.

## Custom Advice

Some questions do not fit a package: a sector-specific rule, a passport requirement in a tender, a data dispute with a supplier, or a second opinion on a provider's offer.

### What you get

- A scoped answer to your question, with the sources behind it

- A short call to walk through it with your team

### Questions it answers

- Does this rule apply to us?

- Is this offer from a passport provider reasonable?

- What should our sector ask of the Commission?

### Often includes

- Expert and stakeholder interviews

- A position paper for a sector body

- A second opinion on a plan or an offer

**A good fit when** you have one concrete question and want a clear answer.

Questions

## About our services

**Q: Do I need all six services?**

No. Each service works on its own. Most clients start with the readiness assessment, because it shows which of the others they need.

**Q: Do you build the passport software?**

We design the passport and stay with your IT team or your passport provider through the build, until a passport passes the Registry&#x27;s checks. For tests we build prototypes; the production system is built and run by you or your provider.

**Q: Which rules do you work with?**

The Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation and the product rules adopted under it, the Battery Regulation, and the EU Digital Product Passport Registry. For a sector rule we have not worked with yet, we say so before we start.

**Q: Can we start with one question?**

Yes. That is what custom advice is for: a scoped answer to one question, with the sources behind it.

## Not sure where to start?

Tell us what you make and where your data lives today. We tell you which service fits, or whether you need us at all.

## Battery passports and the EU DPP Registry: what the 30 October technical package means for your build

URL: https://www.circulartechadvisory.com/insights/dpp-registry-technical-package/
Author: Yvo Hunink de Paiva, CircularTech Advisory
Published: 2026-11-05
Updated: 2026-11-26

The Commission has published a registration API, two authentication profiles and a battery data model for the EU DPP Registry. This is the work plan for battery makers ahead of 18 February 2027, and the reason a successful battery registration still needs testing.

Battery passports become mandatory on **18 February 2027** for electric-vehicle batteries, batteries for light means of transport (LMT) and industrial batteries with a capacity above 2 kWh. The passport itself sits on the manufacturer's side, but Article 77(10) of the Battery Regulation adds a registry step: the battery's unique identifier has to reach the EU DPP Registry. How a company's systems do that by machine was an open question until **30 October 2026**, when the Commission put a technical package on its [DPP resources and documentation page](https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/single-market/digital-product-passport/resources-documentation_en).

**Three things to take away**

- **The building blocks are public.** A registration API, two authentication profiles and a semantic data model for batteries, which is still the only product group with one.

- **Verification comes first.** No organisation registers anything before it is verified, and verification runs on a qualified electronic seal kept on a qualified device.

- **Battery registration is unproven.** The latest User Guide states that successful registration of battery passports is not currently available. Nothing the Commission has published since says otherwise.

At go-live in July 2026 operators had a web form and a file upload, but no API and no data model for batteries. The package fills most of that gap. Where we quote the Commission below, the words are its own.

### The documents

The package adds six documents to the resources page:

- the **API Integration Guide** for economic operators and the matching **OpenAPI specifications** (OpenAPI 3.1, version 1.0.0);

- the **Service Account Technical Integration Guide**, for machine logins to that API;

- the **Self-Hosted Authentication Guide**, for the server that hosts your passport;

- the **Semantic Data Guide** and the downloadable **Semantic Data Artifacts**, with code lists, validation rules and schemas for the core passport and for batteries.

Two older documents on the same page have also moved on. The **User Guide for Economic Operators** is at v1.03, last published on 16 September 2026 (the page itself calls it "v3"). The Commission's guidance on **Digital Batteries Passport data points by category** went to v3.2 on 19 October 2026 and to version 4 on 19 November 2026.

### The data model in eight standards

Most of the model is built on W3C web standards. If the acronyms are new: SKOS describes code lists, SHACL expresses validation rules, RDF is the graph data model underneath, and JSON-LD attaches shared meanings to the keys of an ordinary JSON file. Here is how far the package goes with each one.

| Standard | Role in the package |
| --- | --- |
| SKOS | 17 concept schemes hold every field and every code value. |
| SHACL | 18 shape files (2 core, 16 battery). According to the guide, everything else is generated from them. |
| RDF | Underlying model, shipped as Turtle files. |
| JSON-LD | 5 contexts, stacked from core to product group to sub-group, that tie plain JSON keys to the vocabularies. |
| SPARQL | Appears only as constraints inside the SHACL shapes, for example to test code-list membership. No query service exists. |
| XSD | Supplies the datatypes. XML Schemas are described in the guide, yet no .xsd file is in the download. |
| OWL | Carries version information only: ontology IRI, version IRI, version info. |
| DCAT | Not delivered. A DCAT-AP 3.0.1 catalogue is something the repository "will publish", in the words of the guide. |

None of that changes what you send. Section 2.1 of the Semantic Data Guide puts it plainly: *"The registration process will be requesting JSON data format, as it is the only mandatory data format in accordance with EN 18216:2026."* For JSON the Commission publishes **JSON Schemas** (draft 2020-12, which is not a W3C specification), generated from the shapes, and the Semantic Data Guide says JSON documents are validated with them. Passports in JSON-LD or RDF are validated with the SHACL shapes instead.

The two rule sets are not equally strict. Comparing them file by file, we found three things the shapes enforce and the JSON Schemas do not. A shape pins each battery field to its unit, a voltage to volts for instance, while the schema takes any unit address, including one missing from the code list. Shapes insist on registration per item for batteries; schemas do not. And shapes reject fields that a battery sub-group excludes; schemas let them through. The API guide is silent on which rules the Registry applies to the passport it fetches, so a passport that only clears the JSON Schema is not yet safe.

**Small print that breaks builds**

A passport must name the releases it follows, in contentSpecificationIds: one core release and one product release at minimum, plus a sub-group release if there is one. Language tags need a region subtag, so en-IE is valid and en is not.

Reuse is allowed. The 17 vocabularies and the API specifications carry the EUPL-1.2 open-source licence, and Article 12(7) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1778 makes access to the semantic repository and its APIs free of charge. The shapes, JSON Schemas and contexts have no licence notice so far. If you bundle them in a product, keep the reference to the Commission as their source.

### The registration API

Five operations make up the whole API. One returns the product groups you may register under. One submits a registration. Three read the Activity Dashboard, the Registry's log of tasks, so your system can follow a submission and collect the outcome for each item. You cannot read back, change or withdraw a registration through the API, and the API has no route for verifying your organisation: that still happens in the web interface.

A submission carries between 1 and 100 passports, all of one product group, each with its own UPI. JSON is the only format and 10 MB the ceiling. A battery submission also has to state a sub-group, and here the documents disagree on names. The API guide's examples use EV; the OpenAPI file's examples use EV and LMT; the data model's sub-groups are evb, ind and lmt. No document maps one set onto the other, so read the valid values from the Registry at runtime rather than hard-coding them. Processing is atomic. One failing passport and the whole submission is rejected.

[Figure: A submission of up to 100 passports from one product group, each with its own UPI, goes to the Registry, which fetches and checks every passport. When all pass, each gets its own registration identifier; when one fails, the Registry registers none of them.]

The UPI, the address at which your passport can be found, may now be up to **2,000 characters** long. At registration the Registry goes to that address, downloads your passport and validates it. Hosting therefore comes before registering, not after.

### Two logins, two directions

The package contains two authentication profiles. One covers your software calling the Registry; the other covers the Registry calling your passport server.

### Your software calls the Registry

Only API users need this. An administrator of the verified organisation sets up a service account in the Registry (five per organisation at most) and uploads a public key. Your software then signs a short assertion with the matching private key, which stays with you, and the Commission's login service returns an access token that lasts 15 minutes. The method is OAuth 2.0 private_key_jwt with elliptic-curve keys only; shared client secrets are not offered. Some required settings are not what standard client libraries use out of the box, so your developer should work from the Service Account guide directly.

[Figure: Your system signs a message with its private key and sends it to the Commission's login service, which returns an access pass valid for 15 minutes; with that pass your system calls the Registry API. Once, beforehand, an administrator creates the service account and uploads the public key. People using the web portal log in themselves and do not need this.]

### The Registry calls your passport server

Each passport has a public part and a protected part. During registration the Registry first fetches the passport anonymously and gets the public part. Its second request carries a short-lived token signed by the Commission. Your server validates that token and, if it checks out, returns the protected part as well. The rules are strict: a request without a token gets the public part, and a request with a bad token gets a 401 or 403 error, never a quiet fallback to the public part. Static file hosting cannot do this, so you need either a small server-side check of your own or a passport provider that runs one.

[Figure: Without a pass, a request receives only the public part of the passport. The Registry, presenting a valid Commission pass, receives public and protected parts. A pass that is wrong, expired or meant for another server is answered with error 401 or 403 and never with the public part, which the Registry already fetched in its first call.]

### Access groups the Registry does not serve yet

Public and protected are the only two tiers today, and the Commission's Registry is the only party allowed into the protected one. The battery data model asks for more. It follows Article 77(2) and Annex XIII of the Battery Regulation and places each data point in one of four groups:

- data anyone may see;

- data for persons with a legitimate interest, notified bodies, market surveillance authorities and the Commission;

- data reserved for notified bodies, market surveillance authorities and the Commission;

- data about one individual battery, for persons with a legitimate interest.

Nothing published so far tells a repairer, a recycler or an authority how to fetch groups two to four from a manufacturer's server.

[Figure: Access to the four battery data groups: group 1 (items 1 to 45) is open to everyone. Persons with a legitimate interest, such as repairers, recyclers and second-life operators, reach groups 1, 2 and 4, not group 3 with the test reports. Notified bodies, market surveillance and the Commission reach groups 1, 2 and 3, not group 4 with the data on one specific battery. For groups 2 to 4 there is no published route to the operator's server yet.]

Products under the Ecodesign Regulation will get their access rules one delegated act at a time: Article 9(2) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 leaves the question of who reads or updates which data to those acts, and Article 11 allows the Commission to lay down procedures for the digital credentials of those with access rights. The Self-Hosted Authentication Guide only notes that identifying operators by their unique operator identifier is planned for a later version.

### The CEN/CENELEC standards

The two guides reference IETF internet standards and nothing else. EN 18239 (access rights) and EN 18246 (data authentication), both drafted by CEN/CENELEC JTC 24, are cited neither there nor in Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1778. They also work at another level: the guides cover trust between the Registry and one operator's server, whereas EN 18239 deals with which other parties may read or modify controlled data and EN 18246 with signatures that let you verify both data and issuer. Set against the drafts we have read, there is no conflict. Public data is served without login, and controlled data only after authentication and authorisation. The drafts expect authentication at a high level of assurance; the Registry gets that assurance earlier, at the moment an organisation is verified, for example by a qualified seal or signature under Article 4 of the Implementing Regulation. Neither standard has been cited in the Official Journal so far, and the Commission's [page on harmonised DPP standards](https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/single-market/goods/european-standards/harmonised-standards/digital-product-passport-dpp_en) is where a citation would appear.

### The User Guide on seals

User Guide v1.03 is more explicit than v1.0 on what counts as a valid seal. It has to live on a qualified device, such as a smart card or USB token supplied by your trust service provider, or be applied through a qualified remote-signing service. A certificate held as a software file (.p12 or .pfx) is refused. Anyone still shopping for a seal should check this before paying.

### Batteries: a data model, but no confirmed registration

**Model out, registration unconfirmed**

Six weeks before the battery model appeared, User Guide v1.03 said that successful registration of battery passports is "not currently available". The Commission has not published anything since that reverses this. Run a test registration before planning around it.

Batteries are still the only product group on offer in the Registry, and only at item level. Detergents, construction products, textiles and the ESPR product groups have no semantic model yet.

### Four open points for the rule-makers

We set the battery data model beside version 4 of the Commission's data-points guidance (dated 19 November 2026; like v3.2 it says it does not represent the Commission's official position). Four data points read differently in the two. We may have missed the intended reading, so we put them as questions.

| Data point | Guidance | Data model | Question |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Critical raw materials | Points to Annex X(1) of the Battery Regulation: cobalt, natural graphite, lithium, nickel | Offers the 34 critical raw materials of the Critical Raw Materials Act | Which of the two lists applies to a battery passport? |
| Temperature range for voltage values | To be given "when relevant" | Mandatory in every case | How should a passport express "not relevant"? |
| Separate-collection marking | Yes or no | Accepts "yes" only | Is "no" ruled out on purpose? |
| Rated capacity | Public item 25 repeats another item and is not filled in; restricted item 51 equals item 11 | No item 25, but a restricted rated-capacity field of its own, mandatory for EV and LMT batteries | Fill that field independently, or copy item 11 into it? |

The temperature and marking points are the urgent ones. A passport written to the guidance could be rejected by the data model's checks, so builders need an answer now. If you know what the drafters intended, please tell us.

### A work plan for battery makers

The steps below apply to any product group once its passport rules take effect. Battery makers have to finish them before 18 February 2027.

- **Order the seal now.** Companies need a qualified electronic seal (QSeal), a sole trader a qualified electronic signature (QES). Get it from a qualified trust service provider listed on an EU trusted list, on a qualified device or through remote signing, and sign in PAdES, the PDF signature format. Procurement is the slowest step.

- **Put the passport online first.** The UPI must resolve over HTTPS to valid JSON whose contentSpecificationIds are filled in, because the Registry will download it.

- **Test with both rule sets.** Validate each passport for your sub-group against the JSON Schema and the SHACL shapes until the Commission says which checks it runs at registration. A JSON Schema 2020-12 validator plus an open-source SHACL engine such as pySHACL is enough.

- **Protect the protected part.** Serve the public part to anonymous callers, return 401 for any invalid token without falling back, check the audience against your exact origin, and return 403 unless the caller's organisation identifier matches your policy exactly.

- **Prepare the service account** if you plan to use the API. Store the private key in a hardware security module where possible and schedule key rotation: at most two active credentials, each valid for no more than two years.

Item-level registration multiplies the work. In the web interface one form registers one passport, and one upload holds at most 100, all or nothing. A maker shipping tens of thousands of batteries a year would face hundreds of uploads, which is why the API is the realistic route. Whatever route you take, hosting and the protected endpoint remain necessary, since the Registry fetches the passport and part of the battery data is not public.

### How CircularTech Advisory helps

We take battery makers and their suppliers from the regulation to a passport the Registry will accept. A readiness assessment shows which of your data already covers the 71 battery data points and which of your systems can host and protect a passport. The compliance roadmap puts the seal, the hosting, the validation and the API work in order against 18 February 2027. If you want to know whether your current setup would pass the Registry's checks, that is a conversation we can have this month.

We also help DPP service providers plan the systems their customers will need to meet the Registry's rules.

**Sources**: European Commission, DPP resources and documentation page (technical package of 30 October 2026): API Integration Guide for Economic Operators v1.0 and OpenAPI specifications 1.0.0; Service Account Technical Integration Guide v1.0; Self-Hosted Authentication Guide for Economic Operators v1.0; Semantic Data Guide v1.0 and Semantic Data Artifacts (core 1.0.0, batteries 1.0.0); DPP Registry User Guide for Economic Operators v1.03 (16 September 2026); Guidance Document: Digital Batteries Passport, data points by category v3.2 (19 October 2026) and version 4 (19 November 2026). Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1778; Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 (Batteries); Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 (Ecodesign).

### Frequently asked questions

**Q: Is there an API for the EU DPP Registry?**

Yes, documented since 30 October 2026 in the API Integration Guide and the OpenAPI specifications. It offers five operations: listing product groups, submitting 1 to 100 passports at once (JSON, 10 MB at most, all or nothing) and three Activity Dashboard calls to track a submission and its per-item results. Machines log in through a service account with OAuth 2.0 private_key_jwt.

**Q: In which format do I register a passport?**

In JSON, the only format the Semantic Data Guide makes mandatory, with reference to EN 18216:2026. JSON passports are validated against JSON Schemas; JSON-LD and RDF passports against SHACL shapes. XML only appears as an option for file uploads in the web interface.

**Q: Which semantic web standards does the DPP data model rely on?**

The core is SKOS, SHACL, RDF and JSON-LD. SPARQL is used only within SHACL shapes, XSD only for datatypes (no .xsd files are published), OWL only for version information, and a DCAT-AP catalogue is promised but not delivered. JSON registrations are checked with JSON Schemas (draft 2020-12, not a W3C standard) according to the Semantic Data Guide; the API guide does not state which checks the Registry runs on the passport it downloads.

**Q: Does registering a battery passport work today?**

That is not confirmed. The battery data model came out on 30 October 2026, yet User Guide v1.03 says successful registration of battery passports is not currently available, and no later Commission text reverses this. The Registry offers no product group other than batteries, and those only per item. From 18 February 2027 the passport is required for EV and LMT batteries and for industrial batteries above 2 kWh.
